name: Metronidazole / ivermectin (rosacea creams)

lead: Topical metronidazole and ivermectin 1% cream (Soolantra) are prescription treatments for the inflammatory bumps of rosacea, aimed at a clearer, calmer complexion. They mainly reduce inflamed lesions and redness around them, and do little for persistent flat facial redness, which vasoconstrictors and lasers target instead.

Metronidazole is a nitroimidazole antimicrobial; its benefit in rosacea may come from antibacterial or anti-inflammatory action. Ivermectin acts on invertebrate parasites, and its use rests on the idea that Demodex mites contribute to rosacea. Rosacea overviews describe topical metronidazole as having good evidence for reducing inflammatory bumps; in one cited study ivermectin reduced lesions by 83% over four months versus 74% for metronidazole.

paras: Both are applied to the face as a cream or gel as part of a daily routine prescribed by a clinician, often alongside gentle cleansing and sunscreen. Rosacea overviews describe them as treatments for the inflammatory form, and people combine them with other products when persistent redness is also a concern.

Topical use commonly causes mild local redness, dryness, burning or itching, especially early. Oral metronidazole carries an FDA boxed warning about carcinogenicity in rodents, which applies to the systemic drug, not the topical product. Both topicals require a prescription in the US.

angle.text: Prescription metronidazole and ivermectin creams calm the bumps and inflammation of rosacea, leaving a clearer, less irritated face. They work by settling inflammation rather than shrinking vessels, so they do little for persistent flat redness. Both are well described in rosacea overviews for the bump-type condition.

lead: Topical metronidazole and topical ivermectin are two prescription creams and gels used for the papulopustular (bumpy, inflamed) form of rosacea, a chronic facial skin condition marked by redness, pimple-like lesions, swelling and visible small vessels.[1][2] People use them to reduce the inflamed bumps and the redness immediately around them, which is the part of rosacea that most changes how the skin looks day to day; persistent background redness and visible vessels are addressed by separate treatments such as brimonidine, oxymetazoline and vascular lasers.[1][2][3]

Metronidazole is a nitroimidazole antimicrobial developed by Rhône-Poulenc in the 1950s and first marketed in France in 1960; its benefit in rosacea was reported in a double-blind trial in the Lancet in 1976.[4][5][6] Ivermectin was discovered through work by Satoshi Ōmura and William Campbell, who shared the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, and the 1% cream is sold as Soolantra for rosacea on the premise that Demodex mites contribute to the condition.[7][1]

Rosacea overviews describe topical metronidazole, topical azelaic acid and topical ivermectin as having the strongest support for inflammatory lesions.[3] In one trial cited by Wikipedia, ivermectin reduced lesions by 83% over four months versus 74% for metronidazole, and a 2025 meta-analysis of 21 randomised trials reported ivermectin outperforming both azelaic acid and metronidazole.[1][8] Both products are prescription-only in the US.[5]

subs.h: Rosacea subtypes and where these creams fit
paras: Wikipedia describes four rosacea subtypes: erythematotelangiectatic (persistent redness and visible vessels), papulopustular (bumps and pustules, often confused with acne), phymatous (thickened skin, notably of the nose) and ocular.[1] Metronidazole and ivermectin are aimed at the papulopustular form. A 2021 hospital-medicine review lists 0.75% metronidazole, topical azelaic acid or topical ivermectin as having the strongest evidence for inflammatory rosacea, and brimonidine gel, oral beta blockers or vascular lasers for erythema.[3] Other options named in overviews include low-dose doxycycline, minocycline foam, encapsulated benzoyl peroxide, oral isotretinoin for severe cases, and intense pulsed light or pulsed dye laser for visible vessels.[1][2]

Rosacea affects roughly 1-10% of people by one estimate and most often begins between ages 30 and 50, more commonly in fair-skinned people, though a 2026 review says it may affect 2-4% of Black, Asian, Pacific Islander and Hispanic/Latino populations and is likely underdiagnosed there.[1][9] A Saudi Arabian cross-sectional study of 176 participants found 52.5% reported severe impairment of quality of life, with papules and ocular involvement linked to worse scores.[10]

subs.h: Everyday skin care alongside the creams
paras: Wikipedia's treatment summary lists behavioural measures that accompany drug treatment: a symptom diary to identify triggers such as sun, heat, stress, alcohol and spicy food, SPF 30 or higher sunscreen, avoiding irritants such as alcohol-based astringents and harsh scrubs, and oil-free makeup.[1]

A 1976 double-blind trial in 29 rosacea patients found metronidazole superior to placebo after six weeks (P < 0.02), particularly for papules and pustules, at a time when the mechanism was unknown.[6] Reviews state that topical metronidazole reduces inflammatory lesions and perilesional redness and is generally well tolerated, but does little for persistent facial redness.[1][2]

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 randomised trials covering six topical drugs reported that ivermectin outperformed azelaic acid and metronidazole, azelaic acid outperformed metronidazole, and brimonidine and oxymetazoline reduced facial redness.[8] A 2023 network meta-analysis of 31 randomised trials with 8,226 patients found topical ivermectin and 0.75% metronidazole effective for papules and pustules, while metronidazole 0.75% and doxycycline 40 mg showed no effect on erythema; minocycline 100 mg ranked highest for efficacy overall.[11] A 2026 prospective observational comparison of 23 patients (10 on ivermectin 10 mg/g cream, 13 on metronidazole 1% gel) over eight weeks found both reduced inflammatory lesions significantly; any response occurred in 70% versus 62% and optimal response in 50% versus 31%, with baseline follicular plugs associated with optimal ivermectin response.[12] A 2026 PRISMA review of 15 studies reported benefit for ivermectin, metronidazole, azelaic acid and other options, with mostly moderate risk of bias.[13]
The Medical Letter reviewed the drug options for rosacea in 2024, covering doxycycline, ivermectin, metronidazole, isotretinoin, azelaic acid, brimonidine and oxymetazoline.[14]

Topical metronidazole commonly causes local redness, dryness and irritation, and eye watering if applied near the eyes.[5] Ivermectin cream can cause transient burning or itching.[1] Most topical rosacea options cause local irritation early in treatment.[1]

The FDA label for oral metronidazole carries a boxed warning noting carcinogenicity in mice and rats and advising against unnecessary use, and lists seizures, neuropathy and severe cutaneous adverse reactions as systemic risks.[15] That label concerns the oral drug, not the topical rosacea products. Wikipedia reports that the US National Toxicology Program lists metronidazole as reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen from largely animal data, that IARC classes it as a possible carcinogen, and that the human link is unclear.[5] The same article describes case reports of a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol during systemic therapy and says some studies question the interaction.[5]

Metronidazole is a prodrug activated by anaerobic microbes and protozoa into a reactive radical that damages DNA; because oxygen competes for the activation it has little effect on human cells or aerobic bacteria.[5] Its action in rosacea is not precisely known and may involve antibacterial effects, immunomodulation or both; research suggests it can reduce reactive oxygen species and nitric oxide and dampen NF-kB signalling, lowering pro-inflammatory cytokines.[5]

Ivermectin binds glutamate-gated chloride channels in invertebrate nerve and muscle cells, paralysing the parasite; mammals are largely protected because these channels sit in the brain and spinal cord and the drug does not generally cross the blood-brain barrier at normal doses.[7] Demodex mites are more numerous in some rosacea patients, and a 2007 study linked Bacillus oleronius, a bacterium carried by the mites, to an immune response in 79% of 22 papulopustular patients versus 29% of 17 controls.[1] Other proposed contributors include elevated cathelicidin, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth and a link with inflammatory bowel disease.[1] Ivermectin is also used for Demodex-associated blepharitis, and a 2026 review found oral or topical ivermectin generally associated with reduced mite density and improved symptoms there.[7][16]

Rhône-Poulenc developed metronidazole in the 1950s, commercial use began in France in 1960, and the drug was licensed to G.D. Searle (Pfizer acquired Searle in 2003); the original patent expired in 1982.[4][5] The 1976 Lancet trial by Pye and Burton examined its use in rosacea.[6]

Ōmura isolated Streptomyces avermitilis from Japanese soil in 1970, Campbell's group at Merck developed ivermectin, and it was marketed as a veterinary product from 1981 and approved for human use in 1987.[7] The Nobel Prize committee cited the derivatives' role in lowering river blindness.[7] During the COVID-19 pandemic ivermectin became the subject of widespread misinformation; the FDA, CDC, EMA and WHO advise against its use for COVID-19, and the CDC has warned about overdose from veterinary or external-use products.[7] Topical rosacea ivermectin is a separate prescription product.

Head-to-head randomised trials and meta-analyses place ivermectin ahead of metronidazole for inflammatory lesions, while both show benefit over vehicle or placebo.[1][6][8][11] Registered metronidazole trials for other indications such as bacterial vaginosis, periodontal disease, C. difficile and leishmaniasis are not studies of rosacea.[17][18][19][20]

The creams are mentioned in skincare circles as dermatologist-prescribed options for rosacea bumps and are usually distinguished from products that target flat background redness, such as brimonidine, oxymetazoline and lasers.[1][3] Wikipedia notes that rosacea can affect self-esteem and social life.[1]

lore.intro: Rosacea creams are discussed in skincare circles mainly as the prescription route for inflamed bumps, in contrast to products for flat redness.[1][3]

claims.claim: Ivermectin cream clears rosacea bumps better than metronidazole.
Metronidazole gets rid of rosacea redness.
Topical ivermectin is the same thing as the controversial COVID-era use.
Rosacea is caused by mites and can be cured by killing them.

timeline.event: Metronidazole first marketed in France by Rhône-Poulenc.[4][5]
Ōmura isolates the soil bacterium that leads to ivermectin.[7]
Pye and Burton report a double-blind trial of 29 patients in the Lancet showing metronidazole superior to placebo for rosacea.[6]
Ivermectin marketed as a veterinary antiparasitic.[7]
Study links Bacillus oleronius, carried by Demodex mites, to immune responses in papulopustular rosacea; separate work reports elevated cathelicidin.[1]
Ōmura and Campbell share the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for ivermectin.[7]
Network meta-analysis of 31 rosacea trials (8,226 patients) finds topical ivermectin and metronidazole 0.75% effective for papules and pustules.[11]
Meta-analysis of 21 randomised trials of topical rosacea drugs reports ivermectin outperforming azelaic acid and metronidazole.[8]
